findings.headline: Fair funding review core principles unfavourable to Wigan; transitional support ends at next settlement, requiring further large savings
findings.detail: The council received transitional funding to mitigate the fair funding review impact over three years. This transitional funding is projected to end at the next settlement period, and the council states the core funding formula principles are "not favourable". The removal of this transitional support will create "an increased funding gap which will require significantly more savings to be identified".
findings.matters: After the transitional period, the council faces a structural funding cliff that will require substantial additional savings on top of already-stretched budgets.
findings.figures: Three-year transitional funding ending at next settlement period
findings.quote: Whilst in principle we supported the fair funding review the core principles are not favourable to the Council. Whilst some transitional funding has been made available to mitigate the impact over the 3-year period, this is projected to end at the next settlement period.

findings.headline: £1.627m (11%) of £14.264m savings target at risk of slipping into 2027/28, with in-year achievement uncertain
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 savings target is £14.264m. At Q1, £8.1m had been achieved and the council forecasts £12.637m will be met by year-end, leaving £1.627m at risk. The council attributes the shortfall to timing delays and states work will continue, "but may fall into 2027/28". Given the council's reliance on temporary funding to mask the underlying deficit, slippage in savings requires additional reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: The council is already drawing on temporary corporate funding and reserves to balance the budget; if savings slip, it will need to use additional reserves or find alternative mitigation.
findings.figures: £14.264m savings target, £12.637m forecast delivery, £1.627m (11%) at risk
findings.quote: Although it is predicted at Q1 that £1.627m of the savings target will not be met during 26/27, this is primarily due to timing delays.

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation demand remains significantly above historic levels, forecasting £0.512m year-end overspend
findings.detail: Demand for temporary accommodation remains significantly above historic levels and is being driven up by market inflation. While growth has stabilised in Q1, the service is still forecasting a £0.512m overspend at year-end. The council's homelessness action plan has managed to keep reliance on higher-cost hotel and B&B accommodation low, but the pressure persists.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a growing structural cost pressure for councils; this is one of the few areas where the council shows active mitigation, but the continued forecast overspend suggests the pressure is outpacing the response.
findings.figures: £0.512m forecast overspend, demand remains significantly above historic levels
findings.quote: The largest pressure remains within Homelessness Services, where demand for temporary accommodation remains significantly above historic levels and accommodation costs continue to be impacted by market inflation.

findings.headline: Looked-after children numbers rising 4.3% and EHCP-supported children up 17.8% in a year, driving £3.389m and £1.444m service overruns
findings.detail: LAC numbers increased from 655 to 683 between July 2025 and June 2026. EHCP numbers reached 4,398 in June, an increase of 664 (17.8%) in a year. External residential placements are overrunning by £3.389m and home-to-school transport by £1.444m. The council aims to reduce LAC placement spend by £3.35m by 2028/29 through a Transformation Board, but this area is described as volatile.
findings.matters: Demand in this area is accelerating and reversing prior reductions; placement costs are highly volatile and the council's plan to cut £3.35m depends on disruptive market intervention that has not yet materialized.
findings.figures: LAC numbers +4.3% (655 to 683), EHCP numbers 4,398 (+664 or 17.8% since July 2025), £3.389m LAC placement overspend, £1.444m transport overspend
findings.quote: From an initial sustained reduction following the implementation of the Family Safeguarding model, the number of Children Looked After (CLA) has increased by 4.3% from 655 in July 2025 to 683 in June 2026.

findings.headline: Cumulative DSG High Needs deficit of £25.934m, with £2.594m gap remaining even after conditional government grant, and similar deficits forecast beyond 2028
findings.detail: Wigan's accumulated High Needs Block deficit reached £25.934m by 31 March 2026. The government has offered a £23.340m Stability Grant conditional on approval of a Local SEND Reform Plan, leaving £2.594m uncovered. The council projects similar in-year deficits in 2026/27, and government support for DSG deficits ends 31 March 2028, after which the council may face funding these deficits itself.
findings.matters: This is a structural statutory education funding crisis that the council cannot solve alone and will face a cliff edge in 2028 when government support ends, potentially forcing very difficult choices.
findings.figures: £25.934m cumulative deficit (2025/26), £23.340m conditional grant, £2.594m remaining deficit, similar in-year deficits projected for 2026/27
findings.quote: Each local area was required to submit a Local SEND Reform Plan to the DfE by the 19/06/2026. On condition that the plan is approved by the Secretary of State for Education the Government will award the Council a High Needs Stability Grant to cover 90% of the Authority's overall DSG deficit as at the 31 March 2026. The potential High Needs Stability grant awarded to Wigan Council would be £23.340m, this will still leave a deficit amount of £2.594m

findings.headline: Structural revenue deficit of £8.8m masked by one-off corporate funding and temporary grants
findings.detail: Service budgets are projected £8.8m overspent, but the reported position of £2.868m overspend relies on £5.943m of corporate budget savings and temporary grant funding that are explicitly not sustainable. These temporary measures, not recurrent savings, are what present the council as manageable at year-end.
findings.matters: A lender seeing £2.868m overspend in isolation appears manageable; the underlying £8.8m structural deficit is the real position and signals unsustainable spending relative to base-line funding.
findings.figures: £8.8m service budget overspend, £2.868m reported position, £5.943m temporary corporate mitigation including £0.578m in Financing and Investment Income
findings.quote: Services budgets are projected to be £8.8m overspend however due due to temporary corporate funding we are able to mitigate some of these pressures such that the overall overspend is projected to be £2.868m.

findings.headline: £48.78m (25% of the year's budget) has been rephased out of 2026/27, pushing spend into future years.
findings.detail: The current year allocation was reduced from £239.487m to £190.707m, predominantly due to rephasing and slippage. Significant delays affect Hope School (£9.878m), Woodfold (£5.289m), Haigh Hall (£11.108m), Multi Storey Blocks (£2.1m), and housing schemes. This represents substantial delivery slippage across the programme.
findings.matters: A lender needs to track whether a council can deliver on its capital plans. This scale of rephasing indicates the council is experiencing material delays across its estate. It also means spend is now front-loaded into years 2 and 3, changing borrowing and cash flow profiles.
findings.figures: £48.78m rephased out of 2026/27; £25.003m pushed into 2028/29; Q1 actual spend only £25.146m (13% of revised allocation)
findings.quote: The programme reported to Cabinet at Quarter 4 2025/26 showed a total allocation of £239.487m for the current financial year 2026/27, which has been revised down by a net £48.780m to £190.707m predominantly due to rephasing and reprofiling for known slippage in the programme.

findings.headline: External audit issued disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 financial statements, providing no assurance on the accounts
findings.detail: The external auditor (Forvis Mazars) was unable to complete audit procedures necessary to obtain sufficient evidence by the statutory publication deadline and issued a disclaimer of opinion on 27 February 2026. This means the 2024/25 financial statements carry no external audit assurance, although the council notes this is common across local authorities due to statutory deadline constraints.
findings.matters: A disclaimer opinion means no external verification of the financial statements; while process-driven rather than performance-driven, it indicates timing pressures and removes a key control and assurance mechanism.
findings.figures: Audit report issued 27 February 2026.
findings.quote: We issued our audit report on 27 February 2026. Our audit report included a disclaimer of opinion. This means our audit report did not express an opinion on the financial statements and no assurance was provided. It was necessary to issue a disclaimer of opinion as amendments to the Account and Audit Regulations introduced a statutory deadline for publication of the Council's financial statements.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing issued formal regulatory notice in December 2023 for breaches in gas safety, fire safety, and electrical safety
findings.detail: The council was found to be in breach of the Home Standard for gas safety (including carbon monoxide detectors), fire safety, and electrical safety. A regulatory notice was formally issued by the Regulator of Social Housing in December 2023. Remediation includes operational improvement actions, external consultant review, internal audit review, contract management strengthening, and a stock condition survey programme being procured over 3 years.
findings.matters: Regulatory enforcement indicates control weaknesses in a critical area (tenant safety), requires capital and operational investment to remediate, and carries reputational and regulatory risk if not resolved.
findings.figures: Regulatory notice issued 14 December 2023; stock condition survey programme to be completed over next 3 years.
findings.quote: Following early engagement with the Regulator of Social Housing for the new Housing Standards, it was identified that the Council was in breach of the Home Standard for the following areas: Gas Safety and installation of carbon monoxide detectors. Fire Safety. Electrical Safety. The regulator subsequently issued a regulatory notice in December 2023.

findings.headline: Council must prevent reserves trajectory reaching unsustainable levels, creating dependency on reserve strategies going forward
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that reserves are being drawn down and recognises the need for achievable plans to prevent this trajectory becoming unsustainable. The Section 151 officer reported a 2026/27 balanced budget with reduced need to draw on earmarked reserves and confirmed no Section 114 notice is required, but the underlying concern is flagged.
findings.matters: Reliance on reserves to balance budgets is a fragile position; if reserves deplete to unsustainable levels, the council faces the forced issue of a Section 114 notice or severe service cuts.
findings.figures: No specific reserve balance or depletion rate disclosed; financial resilience identified as 'key risk' for local authorities.
findings.quote: A key part of the financial position for a Local Authority is the adequacy of its financial reserves. In the 2026/2027 budget setting report, it was reported that 'To ensure the trajectory of reserves does not continue to an unsustainable level, the Council must have in place achievable plans to ensure reserves remain robust.'

findings.headline: Children's Social Care remains a major risk to the Council's budget despite growth being added to the allocation
findings.detail: The council identifies Children's Social Care as a significant governance issue and major budget risk. This is monitored by the Director of Finance and Legal through the Children's Services Assurance and Transformation Board. Growth was added to the Children's budget in the 2026/27 budget setting to manage and mitigate demand pressures.
findings.matters: A sustained overspending area that requires budget growth and active management indicates demand or cost pressures that may continue to constrain the council's financial flexibility and reserves.
findings.figures: Updated position set out in March 2026 budget report; specific overspend amounts not disclosed in this governance statement.
findings.quote: A major risk to the achievement of the Council's budget remains within Children's Social Care. On 4th March 2026 the annual Medium Term Financial Plan/Revenue Budget report to Council provided an updated position in respect of this key risk area setting out the growth which has been added to the Children's budget and the actions being taken to manage and mitigate demand.

findings.headline: Delays in receiving valuation data from external valuer required additional audit procedures and cost
findings.detail: The audit fees include £4,200 for additional work arising from delays in receiving information from the Council's valuer. This indicates the Council experienced difficulty obtaining timely year-end valuation data needed to complete financial reporting.
findings.matters: Delays in obtaining key financial data from external vendors suggest control environment issues or resource constraints in the finance function that could affect the quality and timeliness of financial reporting.
findings.figures: £4,200 additional audit fee
findings.quote: Additional work due to the impact of delays in receiving information from the Council's valuer £4,200

findings.headline: Prior period adjustment required, indicating material errors or accounting policy changes in prior year accounts
findings.detail: The audit fees schedule includes £6,900 of additional work specifically for prior period adjustment work. Prior period adjustments are required when prior year financial statements contained material errors or when accounting policies are retroactively changed, suggesting control weaknesses in the financial reporting process.
findings.matters: Prior period adjustments indicate either material past errors in financial reporting or retroactive policy changes, both of which raise questions about the reliability of historical comparatives and the strength of the finance function's controls.
findings.figures: £6,900 additional audit fee
findings.quote: Additional work on the prior period adjustment £6,900

findings.headline: Manchester Airport shareholding valuation depends on uncertain business projections and requires specialist audit procedures
findings.detail: The Council's shareholding in Manchester Airport Group PLC is valued at fair value using financial projections and business assumptions. This is identified as an enhanced risk requiring additional audit procedures including engagement of Mazars' internal valuation specialists to evaluate appropriateness of assumptions and methodology used by management's expert.
findings.matters: Investment valuations based on business projections are inherently uncertain and subject to impairment risk. Material shareholding values can significantly impact reported assets and available reserves.
findings.figures: Shareholding value not disclosed; enhanced risk rating applied
findings.quote: The Council's shareholding in Manchester Airport Group PLC has been valued by a firm of financial experts based on assumptions about financial performance, stability and key business projections.

findings.headline: Property valuations at material risk where assets have not been revalued for up to 4 years
findings.detail: The Council uses a rolling revaluation programme for property, plant and equipment and investment properties. There is documented risk that individual assets not revalued within 4 years may be materially misstated. Additional risk exists because valuations are undertaken throughout the year rather than at year-end, creating potential for year-end divergence.
findings.matters: Property valuations are typically material balance sheet items. Under or over-valued property significantly misrepresents the council's net asset position and debt-to-asset ratios relevant to borrowing capacity and covenant compliance.
findings.figures: Specific values not stated; materiality threshold £23,500k
findings.quote: As a result of the rolling programme of revaluations, there is a risk that individual assets which have not been revalued for up to 4 years are not valued at their materially correct value.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit identified as risk of significant weakness in Value for Money arrangements
findings.detail: The audit fees explicitly allocate £6,300 for additional work on a 'risk of significant weakness relating to the Council's DSG deficit', indicating the audit team has identified concerns about whether the Council has proper arrangements to manage school spending. DSG deficits must eventually be recovered from the general fund.
findings.matters: DSG deficits indicate the schools budget is structurally unbalanced and represents a future draw on council reserves or a governance failure in budget management. This affects the council's overall financial position and resilience.
findings.figures: £6,300 additional audit fee allocation for DSG deficit work
findings.quote: Value for Money work: Additional work arising from risk of significant weakness relating to the Council's DSG deficit £6,300

findings.headline: Reserve balances cannot be verified for prior years due to audit disclaimers, affecting financial sustainability assessment
findings.detail: Because of disclaimed opinions on 2023/24 and 2024/25, the audit team lacks assurance over opening balances for 2025/26, creating particular challenges for validating reserve balances. Reserve balances reflect transactions from earlier years and must maintain the split between usable and unusable reserves required by the financial reporting framework.
findings.matters: Reserve balances are the primary indicator of financial resilience and impact borrowing capacity. Without audit assurance over reserves, the Council's true sustainability and debt service capability cannot be independently verified.
findings.figures: Materiality set at £23,500k; performance materiality £16,400k
findings.quote: This absence of assurance relating to previous years presents particular challenges in relation to reserve balances as these reflect transactions posted in earlier years, including transactions which maintain the split between usable and unusable reserves

findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinions for two consecutive years, recovery to unmodified opinion not expected until 2027-28
findings.detail: The Council received disclaimed opinions on 2023/24 and 2024/25 because insufficient time remained before statutory deadlines to complete audit procedures. Auditors will use a 'proof in total' approach for 2025-26, expected to result in a qualified opinion (not unmodified) until 2027-28. Recovery depends on management meeting agreed timelines and providing prompt responses to audit queries.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions mean auditors could not verify the Council's financial position or the completeness of opening balances. This is a material red flag for lenders assessing financial stability, as the true position cannot be verified.
findings.figures: 2022/23: Unmodified. 2023/24: Disclaimed. 2024/25: Disclaimed. 2025/26 projected: Qualified. 2027/28 projected: Unmodified.
findings.quote: On 27 February 2026, we disclaimed our opinion on the Council's 2024/25 financial statements. This followed on from a disclaimed opinion issued previously in respect of the Council's 2023/24 accounts.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account £2.7m positive contribution is largely one-off, driven by year-end capitalisation of void works; next year faces building services cost increases.
findings.detail: The HRA overperformed Q3 forecast (£0.934m expected, £2.7m actual) primarily due to capitalising 60% of void expenditure, with a large portion processed only in the final quarter. The paper states this is 'one off in nature.' Separately, the HRA will face cost increases next year from a revised building services framework repricing after four years of fixed prices; the council commissioned a review to identify efficiency offsets but outcomes are uncertain.
findings.matters: The HRA's positive outturn cannot be relied on for forward planning. Underlying structural challenge of building services cost increases remains to be resolved.
findings.figures: £2.7m contribution vs £0.934m Q3 forecast, 60% of void work capitalised, adjustment described as one-off
findings.quote: the variance is largely driven by year-end accounting adjustments related to the capitalisation of void property works, with around 60% of void expenditure capitalised substantially higher than previously assumed.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Home to School Transport overspent by £3.207m as child numbers rose 6.4% and daily costs per passenger increased 7%, second-largest service overspend.
findings.detail: This is the third-largest single service cost pressure and exemplifies the pattern of demand and inflation outpacing budget provision across multiple service areas. The paper notes an action plan is in place covering smarter commissioning and travel training, but persistent overspend suggests structural budget risk in this area.
findings.matters: Multiple large service areas (residential placements, home to school transport, adult social care) are simultaneously experiencing similar cost inflation and demand growth, indicating systemic budget risk rather than isolated issues.
findings.figures: £3.207m overspend, 6.4% increase in child numbers, 7% increase in daily cost per passenger
findings.quote: The Home to School Transport service is facing significant cost pressures, with an overspend of £3.207m. This is due to a 6.4% increase in the number of children using transport and a 7% rise in the daily cost per passenger.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: £274.3m (48%) of the capital programme is funded by PWLB borrowing at interest rates described as remaining at 'very high levels', creating ongoing revenue pressure.
findings.detail: Nearly half the £569.4m capital programme is externally financed. The council notes PWLB rates 'continue to remain at very high levels which puts increasing pressure on the Council's revenue budget with regards to the cost of borrowing.' This creates a structural revenue headwind. The paper also notes 'continuing pressures on capital resourcing, specifically with regards to the generation of future capital receipts', limiting alternative financing options.
findings.matters: High-cost borrowing for a large capital programme creates a growing revenue burden that will persist as long as interest rates remain elevated, competing with service provision for budget resources.
findings.figures: £274.3m borrowing out of £569.4m total programme (48%)
findings.quote: Whilst the programme remains in balance and fully resourced, £274.3m (48%) of the total £569.4m programme is resourced from borrowing. Public Works Loans Board (PWLB) interest rates continue to remain at very high levels which puts increasing pressure on the Council's revenue budget with regards to the cost of borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: General Fund Balance of £15.055m is explicitly stated to be low compared with CIPFA statistical neighbours, constraining financial flexibility.
findings.detail: Despite reducing reserve use to £0.6m in 2025/26 (down from prior years), the paper warns that current reserves 'are still considered low when compared with CIPFA statistical neighbours.' The council emphasises it must 'achieve its saving target to maintain the current level of reserves.' Low reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs, demand volatility, or savings plan failure.
findings.matters: Below-average reserves limit financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to external shocks or internal delivery failure.
findings.figures: £15.055m General Fund Balance, £84.8m earmarked reserves, stated to be low vs CIPFA peers
findings.quote: Although the use of reserves has come down significantly in 2025/26, the level of reserves shown are still considered low when compared with CIPFA statistical neighbours. It is imperative the Council through its mission led approach to transformation achieves its saving target to maintain the current level of reserves.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: The £0.065m revenue underspend masks a £13.117m service overspend, offset entirely by £13.182m in one-off corporate benefits rather than recurring savings.
findings.detail: Services overspent by £13.117m. This was matched by £13.182m corporate underspends consisting of: £5m interest underspend from capital reprofiling (timing), £1.488m unbudgeted New Homes Bonus, £1.2m airport dividend, £0.6m additional Section 31 grants. The council explicitly states this approach is 'not sustainable in the long term' and delivery of planned savings is 'essential' for 2026/27. Without these one-offs, the council would report a £13m+ deficit.
findings.matters: The apparent balanced position masks structural deficit risk. Budget dependency on non-recurring income and timing benefits indicates fragile financial management and significant underlying pressure for future years.
findings.figures: Services £13.117m overspend, corporate £13.182m underspend (interest £5m, New Homes Bonus £1.488m, airport dividend £1.2m, Section 31 grants +£0.6m)
findings.quote: As in previous years, the outturn position has been supported by one-off benefits and corporate budget savings, rather than recurring reductions in underlying demand. These measures are not sustainable in the long term, and it remains essential that the Council delivers planned savings and operates within budget in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Children's external residential placement costs rising 11.5% annually, creating £6.043m overspend despite targeted transformation savings.
findings.detail: Average weekly placement costs increased from £6,156 in March 2025 to £6,860 in March 2026. The council has a transformation programme targeting £5m savings over three years and is using costing tools to challenge price increases, but current trajectory shows cost inflation significantly outpacing budget growth. This is the largest single service overspend after corporate mitigations.
findings.matters: A large, persistent overspend in a discretionary-but-necessary service indicates structural budget risk if cost inflation continues to exceed savings delivery.
findings.figures: £6.043m overspend, weekly costs up 11.5% (£6,156→£6,860), transformation target £5m over 3 years
findings.quote: However, costs have continued to rise, with average weekly placement costs increasing by around 11.5%, from £6,156 in March 2025 to £6,860 in March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reaches £25.934m with 10% of in-year deficit unfunded pending government clarification.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit was £9.740m at end 2024/25. In 2025/26, a further £16.194m deficit arose, driven by High Needs Block overspending £18.005m. The government is providing a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% on receipt of an approved SEND improvement plan, but the remaining 10% (~£2.6m of the year's deficit) remains unfunded. The deficit sits outside the main budget under statutory override until March 2028.
findings.matters: A potential £2.6m+ unfunded liability could require reserve drawdown or future budget reallocation, affecting financial resilience.
findings.figures: £25.934m cumulative deficit, £16.194m in-year addition, £18.005m High Needs overspend, 10% unfunded portion
findings.quote: In 2025/26, a further in-year deficit of around £16.194m is expected, again driven by High Needs Pressures which have resulted in an overspend on the High Needs Block of £18.005m bringing the total cumulative deficit to £25.934m.

findings.headline: Internal control observation: accounts receivable and payable control accounts contain unclassified balances
findings.detail: The auditor identified that the accounts receivable control account contained credit balances and the accounts payable account contained debit balances (reflecting overpayments), which should have been reclassified to the opposite side. This resulted in an unadjusted misstatement of £1.452m in the balance sheet (though no net effect). Management will action the recommendation in 2025/26.
findings.matters: While immaterial to the overall position, this indicates a control weakness in reconciliation procedures that could mask or delay identification of genuine debtors and creditors.
findings.figures: Unadjusted misstatement: Dr Current debtors £1,045k / Cr Current liabilities £1,045k; Dr Current liabilities £407k / Cr Current debtors £407k
findings.quote: The Council included debit balances within its accounts payable control account and credit balances within its accounts receivable control account.

findings.headline: Underlying pressures in Children's services and Homelessness continue to drive overspend
findings.detail: The Q2 2024/25 forecast of £8.6m overspend was driven by underlying pressures in Children's directorate and Homelessness. Although pulled back to £2.5m outturn, these service areas remain identified as structural budget risks in the Medium-Term Financial Plan.
findings.matters: Adult social care and homelessness are demand-led and growing nationally; a council experiencing overspend in these areas may face difficulty controlling costs without significant policy or service redesign.
findings.figures: Children's and Homelessness identified as key pressures; Q2 forecast £8.6m overspend, primarily from these areas
findings.quote: This overspend was driven through underlying pressures in the Children's directorate and Homelessness, with the Council forecasting an overspend of £8.6m at Q2 of 2024/25.

findings.headline: Identified budget gaps of £10.3m in 2026/27 and £12.5m in 2027/28 even with council tax rises
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan to 2027/28 identifies gaps of £10.3m for 2026/27 and £12.5m for 2027/28. A 4.99% council tax rise was agreed for 2025/26, raising £7.6m, but these gaps do not assume further rises and indicate the council will need to generate significant new efficiencies or savings.
findings.matters: Forward-looking budget gaps this large signal the council faces sustained pressure and will need to make difficult service reductions or find new revenues over the next two years.
findings.figures: 2026/27 gap £10.3m; 2027/28 gap £12.5m; 2025/26 council tax rise 4.99% raising £7.6m
findings.quote: The budget for the 2025/26 year was balanced with gaps of £10.3m for the 2026/27 financial year and a further gap of £12.5m for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Second consecutive year of revenue outturn overspend at £2.5m, despite Q2 forecast of £8.6m
findings.detail: The council reported a £2.5m revenue overspend for 2024/25, the second consecutive year. This was forecast at £8.6m at Q2 but reduced through additional efficiencies and other receipts including an unbudgeted dividend from Manchester Airport. The overspend was offset through application of earmarked reserves.
findings.matters: Repeated overspend indicates underlying budget pressure or forecasting weakness. While the council pulled it back through one-off items (airport dividend) and efficiency drives, relying on non-recurring income to balance is not sustainable.
findings.figures: 2024/25 outturn: £2.5m overspend; Q2 2024/25 forecast: £8.6m overspend
findings.quote: The Council provided quarterly reports of its financial position to Cabinet across the year, as well as at year end, which reported its revenue outturn position for 2024/25 as an overall overspend of £2.5m. This was the second consecutive year that the Council had reported an overspend.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit surged to £9.7m in 2024/25 and is projected to reach £31.2m by end of 2025/26
findings.detail: The DSG reserve deficit grew from £700k opening balance to £9.7m by year end, driven largely by High Needs Block cumulative overspend increasing from £5.6m to £16.0m. Q2 2025/26 monitoring projects this to reach £31.2m by end of year. If the government's worst-case scenario materialises, the deficit could reach £57.8m by 31 March 2028 when the statutory override expires. The council has a management plan targeting £5m savings in 2025/26 and £6.8m in 2026/27.
findings.matters: This is the largest financial pressure facing the council. While the statutory override allows it to carry the deficit, the scale and trajectory indicate deep structural problems in special educational needs funding that the council cannot solve through its own savings.
findings.figures: Opening deficit £700k; £9.7m at 31/03/2025; Q2 2025/26 projection £31.2m overspend on High Needs; worst-case 2027/28 projection £57.8m
findings.quote: The Council's Budget Monitoring Report for Q2 of 2025/26, taken to Cabinet in November 2025, is projecting the cumulative overspend on the High Needs Block to increase to £31.2m at the end of 2025/26, which would leave an overall DSG reserve deficit of over £20m.

findings.headline: Auditor issued disclaimer of opinion on financial statements due to unfinished audit procedures
findings.detail: The auditor could not complete sufficient audit procedures before the statutory publication deadline, so the audit report included a disclaimer of opinion rather than an audit opinion. This means no assurance was provided over the financial statements. The prior year also received a disclaimer, so opening balances for 2024/25 are also unaudited.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on independently verified financial statements; this is a red flag for any credit assessment and suggests either capacity issues at the council or at the audit firm.
findings.figures: Audit opinion issued 27 February 2026; prior year 2023/24 also disclaimed
findings.quote: Our audit report included a disclaimer of opinion. This means our audit report did not express an opinion on the financial statements and no assurance was provided.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Policy, Prudential Indicators, Capital Programme and Minimum Revenue Provision
findings.headline: Cash balances are declining as the council deploys reserves to fund the gap between capital spending and borrowing.
findings.detail: The council's cash balances are forecast to decline from £42.726m in 2025/26 to £23.416m in 2027/28, reflecting the strategy of using reserves to avoid borrowing at current elevated rates. This draws down a liquidity buffer at a time when the capital programme is at its peak, reducing financial flexibility if circumstances change.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council will retain adequate liquidity to handle unexpected costs or changes to the capital programme, particularly if interest rates do not fall as forecast and it needs to borrow urgently.
findings.figures: Estimated cash invested at year-end: 2025/26 £42.726m, 2026/27 £23.416m, 2027/28 £24.475m
findings.quote: Est cash invested at start of yr 29.890... Est level of cash invested at yr end 42.726... 23.416... 24.475

findings.paper_title: Treasury Policy, Prudential Indicators, Capital Programme and Minimum Revenue Provision
findings.headline: The council's strategy depends on a series of interest rate forecasts that carry material downside risks.
findings.detail: The council's under-borrowing position assumes rates will fall gradually through 2026 and beyond. However, the document identifies seven explicit risks to this: inflation persisting longer than expected, tight labour markets, volatile gilt yields, global fiscal pressures, market expectations being too optimistic, government fiscal policy changing course, and geopolitical shocks. Any of these could prevent the assumed rate cuts, leaving the council borrowing at higher-than-forecast costs.
findings.matters: The affordability of the capital programme rests on a rate forecast that the council itself identifies as subject to material downside risk. A lender needs to understand the council's fallback if this forecast is wrong.
findings.figures: Bank Rate currently 3.75%, forecast to fall gradually; risks include 'only one further cut by mid-2026, potentially bringing the Base Rate to around 3.50%' if expectations prove 'overly optimistic'
findings.quote: Inflation may prove more persistent than expected, delaying the pace of additional Base Rate cuts if underlying price pressures fail to ease as projected.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Policy, Prudential Indicators, Capital Programme and Minimum Revenue Provision
findings.headline: Part of the capital programme is funded by capital receipts from asset sales, which are uncertain and could leave a funding gap.
findings.detail: The council is funding part of its capital programme (£14.095m in 2026/27) from capital receipts—the proceeds of selling council assets. The council explicitly identifies this as a risk: if assets do not sell as planned, the funding falls away and schemes will need to be 'revisited or reprofiled', potentially halting spending or creating a shortfall.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council's capital funding model depends on asset sales that may not happen, and what happens to its finances if they don't.
findings.figures: 2026/27 capital receipts funding: £14.095m; 2027/28: £8.640m
findings.quote: The realisation of capital receipts is also a risk. Certain schemes within the capital programme are funded from capital receipts and if these are not realised then plans will need to be revisited or reprofiled.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Policy, Prudential Indicators, Capital Programme and Minimum Revenue Provision
findings.headline: The council has already experienced significant construction cost inflation and is building contingencies into capital schemes.
findings.detail: The document explicitly states that construction price increases have been significant and that schemes have been reprofiled and contingencies introduced to manage increased costs. This suggests the original capital programme estimates are already under pressure from inflation, and further cost overruns are a live risk as the £240m 2026/27 programme executes.
findings.matters: If construction costs continue to inflate faster than contingencies allow, schemes will either need to be cut or the council will need additional funding, creating a potential deficit.
findings.figures: 2026/27 capital programme £240.077m, with contingencies for construction inflation already embedded
findings.quote: Construction price increases continue to be significant. A number of schemes have been reprofiled and contingencies introduced to meet the increased costs of construction.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Policy, Prudential Indicators, Capital Programme and Minimum Revenue Provision
findings.headline: Capital spending is planned to nearly double in 2026/27, with borrowing more than doubling, while betting on interest rates falling.
findings.detail: The capital programme is projected at £240.077m in 2026/27, compared to £122.953m in 2025/26—a 96% increase. Borrowing requirement rises from £49.902m to £106.018m. The council is deliberately maintaining an under-borrowed position, using cash reserves instead of borrowing, on the assumption that rates will fall from their current levels. If rates remain elevated or inflation persists, this strategy exposes the council to higher-than-forecast borrowing costs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council can afford this capital programme if rates do not fall as expected, and whether the underlying spending plans are deliverable.
findings.figures: 2025/26 capital: £122.953m, 2026/27 capital: £240.077m; 2025/26 borrowing: £49.902m, 2026/27 borrowing: £106.018m; 5yr PWLB rate forecast 4.10%
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (through the CFR), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels

findings.paper_title: Budget 2026/27, Council Tax Setting and Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 – 2028/29
findings.headline: Wigan faces fastest ageing population in Greater Manchester with 60% increase forecast in over-85s by 2030
findings.detail: Adult social care demand is forecast to grow significantly. Wigan has the fastest ageing population in Greater Manchester, with numbers forecast to rise 20% for 65+ and 60% for 85+ by 2030. Obesity levels in the over-65 population are also set to increase significantly, bringing greater health and mobility issues. Additionally, the council is seeing increased volume and complexity of younger adults requiring long-term care, particularly those transitioning from children's services.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the largest demand-driven pressure on council budgets. A 60% increase in the over-85 population is outside the council's control and will drive costs regardless of budget planning. The MTFP allocates growth of £13.954m (2026/27), £8.6m (2027/28), £7.2m (2028/29) but may underestimate the actual trajectory.
findings.figures: 20% increase forecast in 65+ population by 2030; 60% increase in 85+ population by 2030; allocated growth £13.954m (2026/27), £8.6m (2027/28), £7.2m (2028/29)
findings.quote: Wigan has the fastest ageing population in Greater Manchester, with the numbers of older people in the Borough forecast to rise by 20% for 65+ and 60% for 85+ by 2030.

findings.paper_title: Budget 2026/27, Council Tax Setting and Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 – 2028/29
findings.headline: Home to school transport projected to overspend by £2.8m, driven by 98% increase in EHCP numbers since 2018/19
findings.detail: Home to school transport service is forecast to overspend by £2.8m. The primary driver is a 98% increase in Education Health Care Plans (EHCPs) in Wigan since 2018/19 — significantly above North West average (96%) and England average (80%). The acceleration continues, with 21% growth from 2023/24 to 2024/25 compared to 12% North West and 11% nationally.
findings.matters: Transport costs for children with EHCPs are non-discretionary and growing faster than the council can absorb. The 98% historical growth and 21% recent acceleration suggest this pressure will persist and may not be fully captured in current forecasts.
findings.figures: Projected overspend £2.8m; 98% EHCP increase since 2018/19; 21% increase 2023/24 to 2024/25
findings.quote: The Home to School Transport service is projected to overspend by £2.8m.

findings.paper_title: Budget 2026/27, Council Tax Setting and Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 – 2028/29
findings.headline: Wigan's 3-year funding increase of 8.7% is substantially below national average of 15.5%
findings.detail: Over 2026/27 to 2028/29, Wigan's Core Spending Power increases by 8.7% compared to national average of 15.5%. For 2026/27 specifically, the 6.1% increase is only achievable if the council takes the full 4.99% council tax rise; without it, funding falls permanently. The report notes Wigan's increase is 'below average when compared to other Metropolitan and Upper Tier authorities.'
findings.matters: Underfunding relative to peers means the council must cut deeper or find larger efficiencies to deliver same outcomes. This weakens resilience and increases risk that transformation plans will not deliver assumed savings.
findings.figures: Wigan CSP increase 8.7% (2026-2029) vs national average 15.5%; annual increase 2026/27 is 6.1%; council tax rise required £4.872m (2.99%) + £3.258m (2% ASC precept)
findings.quote: Wigan's Core Spending Power to 2028/29 increases by 8.7%. This compares to the national average of 15.5%.

findings.paper_title: Budget 2026/27, Council Tax Setting and Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 – 2028/29
findings.headline: £106m borrowing requirement for 2026/27 in environment where interest rates remain elevated for longer-term debt
findings.detail: Treasury Management strategy identifies borrowing requirement of £106.018m for 2026/27. This represents a shift from internal borrowing (using cash balances) to external PWLB borrowing as internal funds deplete and major regeneration schemes begin construction. The budget acknowledges that whilst interest rates are falling from peaks, they remain high particularly for longer-term borrowing, presenting a material risk to revenue budgets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand debt servicing capacity. At elevated rates, £106m new external borrowing increases revenue pressure. Any delay to capital receipts or asset sales would worsen the position.
findings.figures: Borrowing requirement £106.018m for 2026/27; growth to revenue budget for interest costs and debt repayment £5.384m (2026/27), £3.297m (2027/28), £1.105m (2028/29)
findings.quote: Treasury Management report identifies a borrowing requirement for 2026/27 of £106.018m.

findings.paper_title: Budget 2026/27, Council Tax Setting and Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 – 2028/29
findings.headline: Wigan's useable revenue reserves position is more adverse than comparable authorities
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that its useable revenue reserves (URR) as a proportion of Core Spending Power, and the trajectory of use, are both worse than other Metropolitan and Upper Tier authorities. This reflects post-COVID drawdown of reserves to address systemic pressures. The Section 151 Officer notes the proposed plan must address 'structural usage through base budget growth' — acknowledging this is unsustainable.
findings.matters: Weak reserve positions are an early warning sign of financial stress. That Wigan's position is worse than peers, combined with emerging budget gaps in 2027/28, means the council has less buffer for unexpected demand or funding changes.
findings.figures: No absolute reserve figures disclosed; council benchmarks itself as worse than comparable authorities on URR trajectory
findings.quote: Wigan's remaining useable revenue reserves (URR) as a proportion of CSP (Core Spending Power), and the trajectory of use are both more adverse than the position of other comparable authorities

findings.paper_title: Budget 2026/27, Council Tax Setting and Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 – 2028/29
findings.headline: SEND deficit of £14.285m relies on statutory override expiring end of 2027/28, creating contingent liability
findings.detail: High Needs Block forecast to overspend by £14.285m in 2026/27, protected by a Ministry-extended SEND deficit statutory override that shields the general fund until end of 2027/28. Government will cover 90% of deficits accrued through 2025/26 (payable Autumn 2026), but from 2028/29 onwards the override expires and councils will be subject to government support described only as 'appropriate and proportionate' — no guarantee of full funding.
findings.matters: The council is exposed to a £14.285m contingent liability if government support does not fully cover deficits after the override expires in 2027/28. Special needs demand grows nationally and is cost-driving, outside the council's control.
findings.figures: High Needs Block forecast overspend £14.285m for 2026/27; 90% of accumulated deficit to be covered by grant from Autumn 2026
findings.quote: The High Needs Block continues to overspend, with the forecast being £14.285m for 2026/27 (reported to Schools Forum 15/01/2026).

findings.paper_title: Budget 2026/27, Council Tax Setting and Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 – 2028/29
findings.headline: Children's social care carrying £12m in-year overspend that allocated growth does not address
findings.detail: Current Q3 forecast shows a £12m overspend in children's services. The MTFP allocates growth of £12.6m (2026/27), £3.7m (2027/28), and £3m (2028/29), but the budget narrative indicates this is set at levels that maintain the transformation challenge rather than eliminate the structural pressure. The cost of external residential placements and complexity of cases continue to drive demand above assumptions.
findings.matters: A £12m current overspend in a statutory safeguarding service is material. The growth allocation does not match the overspend size, suggesting continued reliance on in-year management or reserves drawdown.
findings.figures: Current overspend £12m; allocated growth £12.6m (2026/27), £3.7m (2027/28), £3m (2028/29); looked after children 648 (down from 671)
findings.quote: As seen within the Q3 report the current overspend on the budget is £12m.

findings.paper_title: Budget 2026/27, Council Tax Setting and Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 – 2028/29
findings.headline: Budget gaps of £974k in 2027/28 and £4.7m in 2028/29 remain unfunded despite transformation savings
findings.detail: While 2026/27 is balanced with £14.264m in identified savings, the MTFP shows remaining unfunded gaps in later years as transitional funding protections withdraw. The 2027/28 gap is £974k and 2028/29 is £4.744m, despite identified savings of £10.009m and £3.965m respectively. This signals that the council has not yet found solutions to close the structural deficit beyond the next year.
findings.matters: A lender needs credible plans to close emerging deficits. Gaps that widen despite transformation efforts suggest either forecasts are optimistic or further service cuts will be needed.
findings.figures: 2027/28 remaining gap £974k, 2028/29 remaining gap £4.744m; Budget gaps before savings £10.983m and £8.709m respectively
findings.quote: Remaining Budget Gap 0 974 4,744

findings.headline: Council has zero reliance on commercial property returns to fund services
findings.detail: Despite holding commercial assets including industrial units, office buildings, shops, and a Manchester Airport Group stake, the council explicitly states: 'There is currently no reliance on commercial returns to support service activity.' Commercial investment is pursued for economic development and regeneration, with financial returns being secondary.
findings.matters: Zero reliance on commercial income means no hidden funding dependency on property valuations or rental performance; reduces risk but also confirms this asset portfolio provides no offset to capital spending pressures.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: There is currently no reliance on commercial returns to support service activity.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account £26m principal debt repayment due in 2027/28
findings.detail: Section 8.2 states that the 2027/28 Minimum Revenue Provision of £41.121m 'includes HRA which has a repayment in 27/28 of £26m'. This is a material HRA debt principal repayment, representing 63% of that year's total MRP and requiring specific revenue provision from housing rental income or general fund support.
findings.matters: A £26m HRA debt repayment is a discrete revenue obligation in 2027/28 that must be funded from rents or general support and directly reduces that year's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: HRA repayment 2027/28 £26m; MRP & Other Revenue Contributions 2027/28 £41.121m
findings.quote: The MRP estimates for the next three years are shown in the table below this includes HRA which has a repayment in 27/28 of £26m.

findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales severely constrained and declining to £1m by 2028/29
findings.detail: Capital receipts fall from £4.012m in 2025/26 to £1.000m in 2028/29. The council explains the decline stating: 'However, the present economic climate has significantly restrained the level of resources the Council is able to generate locally.' Receipts fund 'the priority rolling programme of capitalised repairs as well as any emergencies', so declining proceeds directly constrain asset maintenance capacity and emergency response capability.
findings.matters: Severely constrained asset sale proceeds force dependence on external grants and borrowing; removes self-help funding and reduces financial autonomy; increases exposure to government funding volatility.
findings.quote: However, the present economic climate has significantly restrained the level of resources the Council is able to generate locally.

findings.headline: Capital reserves depleted to zero by end of 2027/28
findings.detail: The capital programme financing table shows capital reserves contributing £20.472m in 2025/26, £15.500m in 2026/27, then £0.000m in both 2027/28 and 2028/29. After 2026/27, the council will have exhausted all capital reserves and depends entirely on external funding (grants, receipts, contributions) for any capital expenditure.
findings.matters: Loss of reserves eliminates the buffer for emergencies, programme slippage, or capital opportunities and leaves the council entirely dependent on external funding sources it does not control.
findings.quote: Capital Reserves 20.472 15.500 0.000 0.000

findings.headline: Capital programme spikes to £240m in 2026/27, nearly doubling prior year spend
findings.detail: The summary capital programme table shows total capital expenditure of £240.077m in 2026/27 compared to £122.953m in 2025/26, a 95% increase. Largest allocations are to Economy & Regeneration (£91.979m), Children & Young People (£37.278m), and Housing HRA (£58.394m). This represents a material one-year investment concentration before falling to £148.443m in 2027/28.
findings.matters: A doubling of annual capital spend in a single year creates cash management challenges and funding pressure; if receipts or grants underperform, the council will struggle to deliver the programme or will need to incur additional borrowing.

news_drafts.headline: Fair funding review core principles unfavourable to Wigan; transitional support ends at next settlement, requiring further large savings
news_drafts.lead: After the transitional period, the council faces a structural funding cliff that will require substantial additional savings on top of already-stretched budgets.

news_drafts.headline: £1.627m (11%) of £14.264m savings target at risk of slipping into 2027/28, with in-year achievement uncertain
news_drafts.lead: The council is already drawing on temporary corporate funding and reserves to balance the budget; if savings slip, it will need to use additional reserves or find alternative mitigation.

news_drafts.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation demand remains significantly above historic levels, forecasting £0.512m year-end overspend
news_drafts.lead: Homelessness is a growing structural cost pressure for councils; this is one of the few areas where the council shows active mitigation, but the continued forecast overspend suggests the pressure is outpacing the response.
